meaning: To wait idly for opportunities instead of taking initiative. To rely on chance or past luck rather than making an effort.
origin: A farmer in the State of Song saw a rabbit crash into a tree stump and die. He gave up farming and waited by the stump every day for more rabbits, becoming a laughingstock.
example_zh: 不要守株待兔，机会要靠自己去争取。
example_en: Don't just wait by the stump for a rabbit—go out and earn your opportunities.

meaning: To ruin something by adding unnecessary details. Doing extra work that ends up making things worse instead of better.
origin: In a drinking contest, the first man to finish drawing a snake added feet to his drawing to show off, and lost the prize to the second man who pointed out snakes have no feet.
example_zh: 报告已经很完善了，再加这些数据就是画蛇添足。
example_en: The report is already perfect; adding these extra figures is just drawing feet on a snake.

meaning: A person with a narrow worldview who thinks they know everything, unaware of the vast world outside.
origin: A frog living at the bottom of a well believed the sky was only as big as the opening of the well, until a sea turtle told him of the boundless ocean.
example_zh: 你没出过国，简直是井底之蛙。
example_en: You've never been abroad—you're like a frog at the bottom of a well.

meaning: To stubbornly hold onto outdated methods or ideas, ignoring that circumstances have changed.
origin: A man dropped his sword from a moving boat and carved a mark on the boat's side. When the boat stopped, he dove in where the mark was, but the boat had moved while the sword had not.
example_zh: 现在市场变了，你的旧策略就是刻舟求剑。
example_en: The market has changed—sticking to your old strategy is like carving the boat to find the sword.

meaning: To pursue a goal through completely wrong methods. Trying to achieve something in a way that can never work.
origin: Mencius told King Xuan of Qi that trying to rule the world through military force was like climbing a tree to catch fish—it would never succeed.
example_zh: 想靠买彩票致富，简直是缘木求鱼。
example_en: Hoping to get rich by buying lottery tickets is like climbing a tree to catch fish.

meaning: To waste one's words or efforts on someone who cannot understand or appreciate them. Talking over someone's head.
origin: A musician played beautiful music for a cow, but the cow only cared about eating grass—the music was wasted on a listener who couldn't understand it.
example_zh: 跟他讲哲学就是白费口舌，对牛弹琴。
example_en: Explaining philosophy to him is like playing the lute to a cow—a waste of breath.

meaning: To contradict oneself. Saying or doing things that cannot both be true at the same time.
origin: A man sold a spear that could pierce anything and a shield that nothing could pierce. When asked what would happen if the spear struck the shield, he had no answer.
example_zh: 你的话自相矛盾，无法自圆其说。
example_en: Your statements are self-contradictory—you can't have it both ways.

meaning: A loss may turn out to be a gain, and vice versa. Fortune and misfortune are interconnected and hard to judge in the moment.
origin: An old man on the frontier lost his horse. Neighbors consoled him, but he said 'How do you know this isn't a blessing?' The horse returned with a fine stallion. The story continues with fortunes reversing repeatedly.
example_zh: 没拿到录用通知别太难过，塞翁失马焉知非福。
example_en: Don't be too upset about not getting the offer—a loss may be a blessing in disguise.

meaning: It's never too late to fix a problem. Taking corrective action after damage has occurred is still worthwhile.
origin: A shepherd lost a sheep because his pen had a hole. His neighbor said it was too late to fix it, but the shepherd replied that fixing it now would prevent losing more sheep later.
example_zh: 虽然晚了，但亡羊补牢，为时未晚。
example_en: It's late, but better late than never—mending the pen after losing the sheep still helps.

meaning: To claim to like something but actually fear it when confronted with the real thing. Pretended affection that melts under reality.
origin: Lord Ye claimed to love dragons and decorated his whole house with dragon motifs. When a real dragon came to visit him, he was terrified and fled.
example_zh: 你说喜欢挑战，结果真遇到就跑了，真是叶公好龙。
example_en: You claim to love challenges, but run away when one actually appears—true Lord Ye loving dragons.

meaning: Perfectly done, with no flaws or gaps. Flawless execution or design.
origin: A heavenly weaver's garments had no seams, as they were woven from clouds—unlike earthly clothes made by human hands.
example_zh: 这个计划安排得天衣无缝。
example_en: The plan was arranged flawlessly, with no gaps.

meaning: Perseverance and determination can overcome seemingly impossible obstacles. Steady effort over generations accomplishes great things.
origin: An old man named Yu Gong decided to move two mountains blocking his doorway. Despite ridicule, he and his descendants dug daily, eventually moving the gods to pity, who sent angels to carry the mountains away.
example_zh: 只要坚持不懈，愚公移山也能成功。
example_en: With relentless persistence, even moving mountains is possible—the foolish old man's way.

meaning: The finishing touch that brings a work to life. A critical detail that elevates something from good to great.
origin: A painter painted four dragons on a temple wall but left out their eyes, claiming that with eyes they would fly away. Skeptics insisted, so he painted eyes on two—and they soared into the sky in a thunderstorm.
example_zh: 最后这句话是画龙点睛之笔。
example_en: This final sentence is the dotting of the dragon's eyes—the touch that brings it all to life.

meaning: To ruin something by rushing it. Trying to speed up a natural process and ending up destroying it.
origin: An impatient farmer pulled his rice seedlings upward to make them grow faster. He returned home exhausted but proud, only to find his seedlings withered the next day.
example_zh: 教育孩子不能拔苗助长。
example_en: Don't rush a child's education—pulling seedlings to help them grow only kills them.

meaning: An irresistible force or trend. Something so powerful that nothing can stand in its way.
origin: From classical military writings describing a victorious army's unstoppable momentum.
example_zh: 这股技术革命的浪潮势不可挡。
example_en: The wave of technological revolution is unstoppable.

meaning: To amaze everyone with a single brilliant act. Achieving sudden fame or success after a period of obscurity.
origin: King Zhuang of Chu was said to have been silent for three years before suddenly reforming the state and becoming a hegemon. A bird that doesn't fly for three years will soar to the sky when it finally does.
example_zh: 他这次比赛一鸣惊人，夺得冠军。
example_en: He stunned everyone by winning the championship—a single astonishing cry.

meaning: Beyond cure; a problem so deeply rooted it cannot be fixed. Originally referred to terminal illness.
origin: From the Zuo Zhuan: a doctor examined the Duke of Jin and declared his illness had entered the gao and huang regions (above and below the heart), where medicine could not reach.
example_zh: 这家公司的腐败已经病入膏肓。
example_en: The corruption in this company has reached the incurable stage.

meaning: To be in an extremely uncomfortable or anxious position. Feeling restless and uneasy.
origin: From the story of Du Xi in the Jin Dynasty, who was so upright that he felt like he was sitting on a needle mat when in the presence of corrupt officials.
example_zh: 等面试结果的时候，他如坐针毡。
example_en: Waiting for the interview result, he felt like he was sitting on a needle mat.

meaning: To have an insatiable thirst for learning. Studying endlessly without growing tired of it.
origin: From the Analects of Confucius: 'To study and not be satiated, to teach and not grow weary—what difficulty is there in these for me?'
example_zh: 他一生学而不厌，著作等身。
example_en: He spent his life studying without satiation, and his writings equaled his height.

meaning: To rise early and work diligently. Seizing the morning to practice and improve oneself.
origin: Zu Ti and Liu Kun, friends in the Jin Dynasty, would rise at the first cockcrow to practice sword dancing, determined to serve their country.
example_zh: 他每天闻鸡起舞，刻苦训练。
example_en: He rises at the rooster's crow every day and trains diligently.

meaning: To burn one's bridges. Committing fully to a course of action with no retreat possible.
origin: At the Battle of Julu, Xiang Yu ordered his troops to sink their boats and smash their cooking pots after crossing the river, leaving them only three days of food—with no retreat, they fought to victory.
example_zh: 他破釜沉舟，辞职创业了。
example_en: He burned his boats—quit his job to start a business with no way back.

meaning: To accomplish the seemingly impossible through sheer will and effort. Transforming nature itself.
origin: From classical Chinese literature describing supernatural or heroic feats that alter the landscape.
example_zh: 我们有移山倒海的决心。
example_en: We have the determination to move mountains and overturn seas.

meaning: To help others achieve their goals. To actively support another's success.
origin: From the Analects: 'The gentleman completes others' good, he does not complete others' bad. The small man does the opposite.'
example_zh: 我们应该成人之美，互相帮助。
example_en: We should help others succeed—completing their good.

meaning: To be fickle; changing one's mind or desires constantly upon seeing new things. Lack of steadfastness.
origin: From the Book of Rites, describing merchants who changed their wares whenever they saw something new.
example_zh: 他做事见异思迁，难以专注。
example_en: He's fickle in his work, unable to focus—always wanting to move on to the next new thing.

meaning: To weep alone in a corner, isolated from others' joy. Feeling left out while others celebrate.
origin: From a Han Dynasty story where a guest arrived late to a banquet and was placed facing the corner, weeping alone while others enjoyed the feast.
example_zh: 别一个人向隅而泣，加入我们一起庆祝吧。
example_en: Don't weep alone in the corner—join our celebration.

meaning: To grieve for someone whose fate might become your own. Feeling sorrow for the misfortune of a similar person.
origin: From the Yuan Dynasty novel 'Water Margin,' where outlaws grieved for a fallen comrade.
example_zh: 看到同行倒下，他难免兔死狐悲。
example_en: Seeing a fellow entrepreneur fail, he couldn't help but grieve—the rabbit dies, the fox weeps.

meaning: To attempt the impossible overnight. Expecting instant success without the necessary gradual process.
origin: From folk wisdom mocking those who expect unrealistic shortcuts.
example_zh: 创业没有一步登天的事。
example_en: There's no such thing as one-stepping to heaven in business.

meaning: Persistent effort overcomes the hardest obstacles. Small actions repeated continuously accomplish great things.
origin: From a Song Dynasty judicial case where a clerk's small daily thefts added up to a fortune—like water drops eventually piercing stone.
example_zh: 坚持学习，水滴石穿。
example_en: Persist in studying—water drops eventually pierce stone.

meaning: Dumbfounded, completely speechless with shock or astonishment.
origin: From Yuan Dynasty drama describing characters struck speechless.
example_zh: 这个消息让他目瞪口呆。
example_en: The news left him dumbfounded—eyes staring, mouth hanging open.

meaning: To feel at home anywhere in the world. To live freely without being tied to one place.
origin: From the Book of Han, originally describing the emperor's dominion over all the world.
example_zh: 他常年出差，四海为家。
example_en: He travels constantly for work, making the four seas his home.

meaning: To proceed in an orderly, step-by-step manner. Following a planned sequence without rushing.
origin: From classical literature about official selection and procedure, meaning to follow established order.
example_zh: 项目要按部就班地推进。
example_en: The project should proceed step by step, in proper order.

meaning: Unknown to the public; living without fame or recognition.
origin: From classical literature describing those who lived quietly without renown.
example_zh: 他在小镇默默无闻地过了一辈子。
example_en: He lived his whole life in the small town, unknown to the world.

meaning: To know when to stop before going too far. To stop at the right moment.
origin: From the Analects of Confucius, advising moderation and restraint.
example_zh: 玩笑要适可而止，别太过分。
example_en: Jokes should stop where enough is enough—don't go too far.

meaning: The student surpasses the teacher. Successive generations improve upon their predecessors.
origin: From Xunzi: 'Indigo dye comes from the indigo plant, but is bluer than the plant itself.'
example_zh: 徒弟青出于蓝而胜于蓝。
example_en: The apprentice has surpassed the master—bluer than the indigo plant he came from.

meaning: To focus on trivial matters while neglecting the essential. To lose sight of what's truly important.
origin: From the Book of Han, describing agricultural neglect in favor of commerce.
example_zh: 注重包装而忽视质量，就是舍本逐末。
example_en: Focusing on packaging while neglecting quality is abandoning the root for the branches.

meaning: A wide variety; many different kinds of things. Diverse and colorful.
origin: From ancient tactical formations—the 'Five Flowers' and 'Eight Gates' were military formations that later came to represent variety.
example_zh: 市场上的商品五花八门，让人眼花缭乱。
example_en: The variety of goods in the market is dazzling—all sorts of things.

meaning: To hit the nail on the head with a single sentence. To reveal the truth in one incisive remark.
origin: From classical vernacular literature.
example_zh: 他一语道破了问题的关键。
example_en: He broke through to the heart of the matter with a single sentence.

meaning: To bring back from the brink of death. To save a hopeless situation miraculously.
origin: From stories of legendary physicians like Bian Que whose treatments seemed to revive the dead.
example_zh: 这位医生有起死回生之术。
example_en: This doctor has the skill to raise the dead and return life.

meaning: To find new life or opportunity after a period of decline. A second chance at success.
origin: From Buddhist scriptures, where the withered tree blossoming symbolized revival.
example_zh: 退休后他创业成功，枯木逢春。
example_en: After retirement, he started a successful business—dead wood meeting spring.

meaning: In the prime of youth, full of talent and vitality. At the peak of one's powers.
origin: From Mao Zedong's poem 'Qin Yuan Chun - Changsha' describing young revolutionaries.
example_zh: 他们风华正茂，正是干事业的好年纪。
example_en: They are in the prime of youth—the perfect age to build their careers.

meaning: To become even more powerful. Adding strength to something already strong.
origin: From the Three Kingdoms period, describing Zhuge Liang joining Liu Bei's forces.
example_zh: 有了这笔投资，公司如虎添翼。
example_en: With this investment, the company is like a tiger with added wings.

meaning: Rich, varied, and colorful; describing content, activities, or life as being full of variety and interest. It conveys a sense of abundance and diversity that makes something vibrant and engaging. Often used to praise events, cultures, or experiences as multifaceted and stimulating.
origin: The phrase is a modern compound idiom formed from the adjectives '丰富' (abundant, in use since classical times) and '多彩' (colorful, appearing in Tang and Song poetry). Unlike many chengyu tied to a single classical anecdote, it emerged as a fixed four-character expression in early 20th-century vernacular Chinese (baihua) literature, gaining widespread currency in newspapers and essays of the Republican era. It crystallized a long-standing aesthetic ideal in Chinese culture—valuing multiplicity and ornamentation—into a concise expression. Today it is one of the most frequently used descriptive chengyu in modern Chinese.
example_zh: 这个夏令营的活动丰富多彩，孩子们每天都过得很充实。
example_en: The summer camp offers a rich and colorful variety of activities, and the children have a fulfilling time every day.

meaning: Literally 'to open the door and see the mountain,' this idiom means to come straight to the point without beating around the bush. It describes speech or writing that is direct, candid, and gets to the heart of the matter from the very start.
origin: The phrase originates from Tang Dynasty poetry criticism, particularly associated with the poet and critic Yan Yu (严羽) in his work 'Canglang's Remarks on Poetry' (《沧浪诗话》). He praised poems that began directly with their main subject, like opening a door to immediately behold a mountain before one, rather than circling with ornamental preambles. The image reflects the Chinese aesthetic of clarity and directness in literary expression. Over time it became a widely used metaphor for straightforward communication in both writing and conversation.
example_zh: 他一进门就开门见山地说出了自己的来意。
example_en: As soon as he walked in, he came straight to the point and stated his purpose.

meaning: Describes earnestly and repeatedly seeking out talent or a wise person with great sincerity and humility. It conveys a leader's persistent effort to recruit someone valuable, even at personal inconvenience. Today it is used whenever someone makes repeated, sincere efforts to invite or win over an expert.
origin: The idiom comes from the late Eastern Han Dynasty, just before the Three Kingdoms period. The warlord Liu Bei, eager to restore the Han, learned that the brilliant strategist Zhuge Liang was living in seclusion in a thatched cottage at Longzhong. Despite winter weather and the objections of his brothers, Liu Bei personally called on Zhuge Liang three times before the recluse finally agreed to meet him and lay out the famous Longzhong Plan. Deeply moved by such humility, Zhuge Liang agreed to serve Liu Bei and became his chief strategist, helping found the state of Shu Han. The story is recorded in 'Records of the Three Kingdoms' (Sanguozhi) and later dramatized in 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' (Sanguo Yanyi).
example_zh: 为了请到这位顶尖工程师，公司总经理三顾茅庐，亲自飞到外地登门邀请。
example_en: To recruit this top engineer, the company's CEO visited him in person out of town three times, like Liu Bei seeking out Zhuge Liang.

meaning: An idiom describing something of tremendous impact, scale, or intensity — literally earth-shattering. It is used for events, achievements, sounds, or actions so powerful that they seem to shake the heavens and the earth, leaving a profound impression on everyone who witnesses them.
origin: The phrase is classically traced to the Tang dynasty poet Bai Juyi (白居易), who wrote in his poem 'Li Bai's Tomb' (《李白墓》): 'Pitiful are the bones in this barren grave and exhausted spring, yet once they produced writings that startled heaven and moved the earth' (可怜荒垄穷泉骨，曾有惊天动地文). Bai Juyi used the expression to honor the sublime, world-shaking power of Li Bai's poetry. Over the centuries the phrase escaped its literary origins and came to describe any phenomenon — a battle, an invention, a speech — of extraordinary force and consequence.
example_zh: 这部电影的特效堪称惊天动地，让所有观众都为之震撼。
example_en: The special effects in this film were truly earth-shattering, leaving the entire audience in awe.

meaning: To offer a humble or modest remark in order to prompt others to share their more valuable insights or ideas. The speaker compares their own contribution to a worthless brick while hoping to elicit something as precious as jade from the audience. It is commonly used as a self-deprecating polite opener before presenting an opinion, proposal, or creative work.
origin: The idiom is attributed to the Tang dynasty poet Chang Jian (常建). Legend says Chang Jian admired the poems of his contemporary Zhao Gu (赵嘏) and devised a clever plan to obtain one. He deliberately wrote an incomplete poem on the wall of Lingyan Temple (灵岩寺), leaving the last couplet unfinished, hoping Zhao Gu would come along and fill in the missing lines. Zhao Gu eventually visited the temple, saw the poem, and indeed composed a masterful concluding couplet — far surpassing Chang Jian's verses. Thus Chang Jian's modest lines were the 'brick' and Zhao Gu's brilliant additions were the 'jade.'
example_zh: 我先谈一点粗浅的看法，算是抛砖引玉吧，希望大家畅所欲言。
example_en: Let me share a few rough thoughts first as a modest opener — I hope everyone will feel free to speak up and share their own insights.

meaning: A mindset of accepting everyone and everything that approaches or is offered, without discrimination or rejection. It describes an open, all-inclusive attitude toward people, ideas, or opportunities.
origin: The idiom traces back to the ancient philosopher Mencius (孟子) and the Confucian tradition. In the Mengzi (《孟子》), Mencius advocated a benevolent and inclusive approach to governance, suggesting that a virtuous ruler should welcome all who come seeking guidance or service. The phrase crystallizes the Confucian ideal of boundless generosity—receiving scholars, commoners, and supplicants alike without turning anyone away.
example_zh: 这位老教授对学生来者不拒，无论什么时候来请教，他都会耐心解答。
example_en: The old professor refuses no one—no matter when students come to him for guidance, he always answers patiently.

meaning: To stubbornly insist on doing things one's own way, disregarding the advice or objections of others. It describes a person who acts willfully and arbitrarily, refusing to listen to reason or collective opinion.
origin: The idiom comes from the Records of the Grand Historian (史记·酷吏列传) by Sima Qian. Zhao Yu (赵禹), a strict official during the Western Han Dynasty, was known for his unyielding nature. When colleagues tried to curry favor or soften his rigid enforcement of the law, he paid them no heed. Sima Qian described him as acting alone according to his own will — 一意孤行 — meaning he neither sought allies nor compromised his standards. Originally the phrase carried a somewhat positive nuance of principled independence, though in modern usage it is almost always pejorative.
example_zh: 大家都劝他不要贸然辞职，他却一意孤行，结果落得个两头落空的下场。
example_en: Everyone urged him not to quit his job recklessly, but he stubbornly insisted on going his own way and ended up losing out on both fronts.

meaning: Describes a situation, effort, or endeavor that begins with great energy and ambition but ends weakly or is left unfinished. The vivid imagery contrasts the formidable tiger's head with the thin, feeble snake's tail to convey a dramatic drop-off in commitment or quality.
origin: The idiom emerged from Yuan dynasty vernacular literature and drama, where the striking image of a tiger's head paired with a snake's tail was used to mock those who made grand plans but failed to see them through. It appears in multiple Yuan dynasty plays and popular fiction of the era as a colorful metaphor for inconsistency. The phrase crystallized into a fixed four-character idiom during the Ming and Qing dynasties, when it was widely used in novels such as 《水浒传》 to criticize characters who lacked follow-through.
example_zh: 这个项目刚开始时声势浩大，各部门都投入了大量资源，但几个月后就虎头蛇尾，没人再过问了。
example_en: The project started with great fanfare, with every department pouring in resources, but a few months later it fizzled out completely and nobody bothered to follow up.

meaning: To achieve two goals with a single action. It describes a situation where one effort produces two beneficial results, similar to the English expression 'kill two birds with one stone.'
origin: This idiom traces back to the writings of the Jin dynasty scholar Ge Hong (葛洪) in his work Baopuzi (抱朴子). It is also associated with earlier Han dynasty texts discussing strategic efficiency. The core idea—that a wise person maximizes outcomes by identifying actions that serve multiple purposes simultaneously—was a recurring theme in classical Chinese military and philosophical literature.
example_zh: 每天骑自行车上班，既能锻炼身体，又能节省交通费，真是一举两得。
example_en: Cycling to work every day lets you exercise and save on transport costs at the same time—it's really killing two birds with one stone.

meaning: An event or situation that has never occurred in recorded history; completely unprecedented. It describes something so extraordinary or unique that no prior comparable example exists.
origin: The idiom emerged from modern Chinese usage, gaining widespread prominence after the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. It was frequently used in official discourse to describe the unprecedented scale of socialist construction. Unlike many four-character idioms rooted in classical texts, this phrase was assembled from common characters and popularized through 20th-century political and media language rather than any single classical literary source.
example_zh: 这次疫情的全球蔓延是史无前例的，各国政府不得不采取紧急措施。
example_en: The global spread of this pandemic was unprecedented, and governments around the world had to take emergency measures.

meaning: To deceive oneself by ignoring obvious facts. It describes a person who tries to hide a problem from others while remaining fully aware of it themselves, much like covering one's own ears while stealing a bell.
origin: The idiom originates from the story recorded in the Lüshi Chunqiu (吕氏春秋), a text compiled during the Warring States period under the patronage of Lü Buwei of the Qin state. A thief tried to steal a large bell from a market but found it too heavy to carry. He decided to smash it into pieces, but the ringing sound drew attention. He then covered his own ears, believing that if he could not hear the noise, no one else could either. The story satirizes the absurdity of self-deception.
example_zh: 他以为把收据藏起来就能逃税，简直是掩耳盗铃。
example_en: He thought hiding the receipts would help him evade taxes—it's nothing but deceiving himself.

meaning: A minor flaw or imperfection in something that is otherwise excellent. It describes a situation where something is largely beautiful or satisfactory but has a small defect that detracts from its overall perfection.
origin: The idiom emerged in classical Chinese vernacular literature during the Ming and Qing dynasties. It is notably used in Cao Xueqin's 'Dream of the Red Chamber' (红楼梦, c. 1791), one of China's Four Great Classical Novels, where it appears in contexts lamenting that even the most splendid things harbor small regrets. The phrase reflects a deeply rooted Chinese aesthetic and philosophical sensibility that true perfection is rare, and beauty almost always carries a trace of incompleteness.
example_zh: 这部电影的画面和配乐都堪称一流，只可惜剧情稍显拖沓，真是美中不足。
example_en: The cinematography and soundtrack of this film are top-notch, but unfortunately the plot drags a bit — a real fly in the ointment.

meaning: To lack the strength or ability to accomplish what one wishes to do. It describes a situation where one's ambition or desire exceeds one's actual capacity.
origin: This idiom appears in the "Book of Later Han" (后汉书·班超传), recounting the story of the Eastern Han dynasty general Ban Chao (班超). After decades of defending the western frontier, Ban Chao wrote to Emperor He in his old age, saying that his body was declining and he could no longer carry out his duties as before — his strength no longer followed his heart. The emperor, moved by his plea, eventually allowed him to return to the capital.
example_zh: 我想帮他们完成这个项目，但能力有限，实在力不从心。
example_en: I want to help them finish this project, but my abilities are limited — I simply lack the capacity.

meaning: To feel as though one is personally present in a situation or scene. It describes the vivid, immersive sensation of experiencing something firsthand, as if actually being there rather than merely hearing or reading about it.
origin: The phrase traces its roots to classical Chinese literary aesthetics. While not tied to a single specific historical anecdote, it crystallized as a concept in literary criticism during the Ming and Qing dynasties, particularly in discussions of landscape poetry and narrative fiction. Critics used it to praise works that transported readers so effectively into the depicted world that the boundary between reading and experiencing dissolved. The idiom encapsulates a core ideal of traditional Chinese literary theory: that great writing should make the reader 'personally arrive at the scene.'
example_zh: 读了这本书，我仿佛身临其境，亲眼目睹了那个时代的繁华与衰落。
example_en: Reading this book, I felt as if I were personally present, witnessing firsthand the prosperity and decline of that era.

meaning: To rise rapidly and straight to a high position, like soaring through the blue sky. It describes someone whose career or social status advances swiftly and spectacularly, often with connotations of reaching the upper echelons of officialdom or prominence.
origin: The phrase draws from the classical Chinese metaphor of '青云' (blue clouds), which symbolizes the highest heavens and by extension a lofty official position. The concept appears in early texts such as the 'Zhuangzi', where surpassing the blue clouds represents transcending the ordinary realm. The four-character idiom as we know it took shape in later dynastic literature, used to praise officials who were promoted with exceptional speed — often through the examination system or imperial favor — ascending the bureaucratic hierarchy as if climbing straight into the sky.
example_zh: 他年纪轻轻就青云直上，三十岁便已官至厅局级，令同僚们艳羡不已。
example_en: He enjoyed a meteoric rise at a young age, reaching the director-general level by thirty and leaving his colleagues envious.

meaning: To do everything in one's power and spare no effort in pursuing a goal. It conveys the idea of giving one's absolute best, holding nothing back. The idiom emphasizes total commitment and the willingness to use every last ounce of energy or resources.
origin: The idiom traces its roots to classical Chinese texts. A notable early usage appears in the works of the Han dynasty, where the phrase was employed to describe officials and soldiers who gave their all in service. The concept of '竭' meaning 'to exhaust or drain' is ancient, appearing in texts such as the Zuozhuan and the Han Shu. Over centuries, the four-character combination became a standard expression for wholehearted dedication to any task or duty.
example_zh: 为了攻克这道技术难题，整个团队竭尽全力，连续加班了一个月。
example_en: To overcome this technical challenge, the entire team did their utmost, working overtime for a whole month.

meaning: To speak but fail to keep one's word; to be untrustworthy or insincere in what one says. It describes a person who makes promises or commitments but does not follow through on them.
origin: The phrase derives from classical Confucian teachings on the importance of trustworthiness (信) in human conduct. It appears in the context of the virtue of '信' being one of the five fundamental Confucian moral principles, emphasized by Mencius and earlier in the Analects. The idea that a person who lacks trustworthiness is not fit to stand in society is a recurring theme in pre-Qin philosophical texts.
example_zh: 他答应帮我搬家，结果却言而无信，让我白等了一天。
example_en: He promised to help me move, but he broke his word, leaving me waiting all day for nothing.

meaning: To fail a competitive examination or selection process. It refers to someone who did not make the cut in a ranked list of successful candidates. The idiom is commonly used to describe failing the imperial examinations or, by extension, failing any important test or competition.
origin: The phrase comes from a Song Dynasty story about a man named Sun Shan (孙山), who was known for his witty humor. Sun Shan and a fellow townsman's son both took the imperial examination together. When the results were announced, Sun Shan's name appeared last on the list of successful candidates, while his companion's son failed. Upon returning home, the townsman asked about his son's result. Sun Shan replied with a clever couplet: 'Sun Shan's name is behind the examiner, and your son's name is behind Sun Shan' — meaning both literally and figuratively that the son did not pass. The phrase was recorded in the Song Dynasty collection 'Gu Jin Tan' (古今谭) by Feng Menglong's era or earlier anecdotal compilations.
example_zh: 他连续两年参加高考，都名落孙山，但他没有放弃，第三年终于考上了理想的大学。
example_en: He took the college entrance exam for two consecutive years and failed both times, but he didn't give up and was finally admitted to his dream university on his third try.

meaning: This idiom describes someone who remains steadfast and refuses to give in, no matter how great the pressure or adversity. It conveys an unyielding spirit and firm resolve in the face of difficulties. It is commonly used to praise those who persist in their convictions despite overwhelming odds.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Han Dynasty work "Records of the Grand Historian" (史记) by Sima Qian. In the biography of the loyal minister Jia Yi, the text describes the quality of remaining unbent and unyielding under pressure, using the language "不屈" (not bending) and "不挠" (not yielding). Later literary sources solidified the pairing into the fixed four-character idiom, cementing its association with moral courage and resolute character.
example_zh: 面对种种困难，他始终不屈不挠，最终实现了自己的梦想。
example_en: In the face of all kinds of difficulties, he remained unyielding and ultimately realized his dream.

meaning: Describes a situation where all resources and options have been completely depleted, leaving a person with no way forward. It conveys the sense of being at an impasse or dead end with no escape. Often used in the context of desperate circumstances where hope seems lost.
origin: This idiom comes from a famous poem by the Northern Song dynasty poet Lu You (陆游), titled 'Visit to Shanxi Village' (游山西村). The full couplet reads '山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村' — meaning amid confusing, dead-end mountains and rivers, one suddenly discovers another village beyond the dark willows and bright blossoms. The phrase 山穷水尽 was later extracted to describe the desperate moment before a sudden turn for the better.
example_zh: 资金链断裂后，公司已到了山穷水尽的地步，随时可能宣布破产。
example_en: After the funding chain broke, the company reached the end of its rope and could declare bankruptcy at any moment.

meaning: The truth finally comes to light after a period of uncertainty. It describes a situation where hidden facts are revealed, just as stones at the bottom of a river become visible when the water level drops.
origin: The phrase originates from a poem by the Northern Song dynasty poet Ouyang Xiu (欧阳修), titled '醉翁亭记' (The Pavilion of the Drunken Old Man), written circa 1046 AD. In the poem, Ouyang Xiu describes the seasonal scenery around Mount Langya, writing that when the water recedes in autumn and winter, the rocks beneath are exposed. Later scholars extended the imagery metaphorically to mean the revelation of truth or facts that were previously obscured.
example_zh: 经过长时间的调查，案件的真相终于水落石出了。
example_en: After a long investigation, the truth of the case finally came to light.

meaning: To scramble to be first and fear being left behind. It describes people eagerly competing or rushing forward, unwilling to lag behind others in pursuit of a goal or opportunity.
origin: The idiom comes from Qu Yuan's (屈原) ancient poem 'Li Sao' (《离骚》) from the Warring States period: '众皆竞进以贪婪兮，凭不厌乎求索' — though the exact four-character phrase was later crystallized from this spirit. Another early attestation appears in the classical commentary tradition describing how people vie for advantage. The phrase has been used in its modern form since at least the Tang dynasty, capturing the universal human impulse to outpace one's peers.
example_zh: 商场一开门，顾客们争先恐后地涌进去抢购特价商品。
example_en: The moment the store opened, customers scrambled to rush in and grab the discounted items.

meaning: Things become completely clear at a single glance. It describes a situation where the facts or overall picture are immediately obvious and easy to understand without further explanation.
origin: This idiom originates from the Song dynasty work 《朱子语类》(Conversations of Master Zhu) by the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200). Zhu Xi used the expression to describe how the fundamental principles of things can become immediately apparent when one's understanding is sufficiently clear. The phrase later entered common usage as a general description of anything that is instantly comprehensible.
example_zh: 这份图表设计得很好，数据趋势一目了然。
example_en: This chart is very well designed — the data trends are clear at a glance.

meaning: To be overjoyed, delighted beyond expectation. It describes the feeling of being pleasantly surprised by something far better than one had hoped for.
origin: The idiom traces back to Song dynasty literature. It appears in works such as Su Shi's writings and later Song vernacular fiction, where 望外 referred to outcomes beyond one's expectations. The phrase was widely popularized in Ming-Qing vernacular novels like Journey to the West and Dream of the Red Chamber to describe characters' unexpected joy. Its classical root lies in the concept that true happiness arises when reality surpasses anticipation.
example_zh: 听到自己被录取的消息，他喜出望外，激动得说不出话来。
example_en: Overjoyed at hearing the news of his admission, he was so excited he couldn't speak.

meaning: To engage in empty theorizing about military strategy without practical experience. It describes someone who discusses things abstractly but cannot apply them in real situations.
origin: The idiom originates from the historical Records of the Grand Historian (史记·廉颇蔺相如列传) by Sima Qian. During the Warring States period, Zhao Kuo, son of the famous Zhao general Zhao She, was well-versed in military texts and could discuss strategy fluently on paper. King of Zhao appointed him commander to replace the ailing general Lian Po, but at the Battle of Changping (260 BC), Zhao Kuo's rigid book knowledge led to a catastrophic defeat and the loss of 400,000 Zhao soldiers.
example_zh: 光靠书本知识纸上谈兵是解决不了实际问题的，必须深入基层调查研究。
example_en: Relying solely on book knowledge and empty talk won't solve practical problems — you must go deep into the grassroots and conduct real investigations.

meaning: Describes an eager, enthusiastic readiness to attempt something new or take on a challenge. The person is practically itching to have a go, full of anticipation and restless energy. It carries a positive, spirited connotation rather than a cautious one.
origin: This idiom traces back to the ancient text 《诗经·大雅·旱麓》 (Book of Odes, Greater Odes, 'Han Lu'), where the phrase '跃跃毚兔' describes a lively, bounding hare. Later writers extended the imagery of leaping eagerness to human behavior, and the expression evolved into '跃跃欲试' to capture the feeling of being so eager that one is ready to spring into action at any moment.
example_zh: 听到这个新项目的消息后，大家都跃跃欲试，纷纷报名参加。
example_en: Hearing about this new project, everyone was itching to give it a try and eagerly signed up to participate.

meaning: A dazzling array of beautiful things; an impressive collection of fine items filling one's field of vision. It describes a scene where exquisite, high-quality objects are displayed in great abundance, delighting the observer's eyes.
origin: The phrase originates from Jin Dynasty scholar Lu Ji's (陆机) "Wen Fu" (文赋, Ode to Literature), where he wrote of beautiful things being displayed before one's eyes. The individual characters 琳 and 琅 both refer to types of fine jade, symbolizing preciousness. Over centuries the idiom evolved from describing literary excellence to broadly denoting any magnificent assortment of beautiful objects or rich offerings.
example_zh: 走进博物馆的展厅，各种精美的古代玉器琳琅满目，令人叹为观止。
example_en: Walking into the museum's exhibition hall, the dazzling array of exquisite ancient jade artifacts left visitors in awe.

meaning: To be half-hearted, indecisive, or easily distracted. It describes someone who lacks focus and keeps changing their mind or shifting their attention between different things.
origin: This idiom appears in classical texts such as the Daoist scripture Taishang Ganying Pian (太上感应篇) and later vernacular literature. The phrase uses the numbers three and two metaphorically — not literally — to convey a scattered, unstable state of mind. It contrasts with the ideal of single-minded dedication (一心一意) praised in Confucian thought.
example_zh: 做事三心二意的人，往往什么事都做不好。
example_en: People who do things half-heartedly usually can't do anything well.

meaning: To use lame or forced arguments to insist on being right; to try to win a debate through sophistry rather than sound reasoning. It describes someone who twists logic and clings to their position despite having no valid basis for their claims.
origin: This idiom emerged from classical Chinese literary discourse, with early usage found in Ming dynasty vernacular works such as 《醒世恒言》and the classic novel 《红楼梦》. The phrase captures the long-standing Confucian critique of those who rely on rhetorical force rather than moral and logical substance. Classical scholars frequently condemned the practice of using clever but hollow words to claim the mantle of reason, making this concept a recurring theme in Chinese literary and philosophical traditions.
example_zh: 他明明做错了事，却还在那里强词夺理，就是不肯认错。
example_en: He had clearly done the wrong thing, yet he kept making lame arguments and simply refused to admit his mistake.

meaning: Describes something that has been completely renewed or transformed, taking on an entirely fresh and bright appearance. It conveys a thorough, striking change that leaves the subject looking or feeling brand new, often implying improvement.
origin: The idiom traces back to Song dynasty scholar Zhu Xi (朱熹), who wrote in his commentary on the I Ching: "须是焕然一新，如混沌初开" (It must be radiant and completely new, like the primordial chaos first parting). Later, Song dynasty official Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹) also used the expression in literary contexts. The key character 焕 refers to a brilliant, radiant quality, emphasizing that the transformation is not merely new but luminous and impressive.
example_zh: 经过彻底装修后，老房子焕然一新，简直认不出来了。
example_en: After a thorough renovation, the old house took on a completely new look — you could barely recognize it.

meaning: An inescapable trap or dragnet that leaves no way out. It describes a situation where someone is completely surrounded or caught, with every avenue of escape blocked.
origin: The idiom traces back to ancient Chinese Taoist cosmology, where 天网 referred to the vast net of heaven spread across the sky. It appears in Chapter 73 of the Dao De Jing (道德经) by Laozi: '天网恢恢，疏而不失' (The net of heaven is vast; though its mesh is wide, nothing slips through). The paired form 天罗地网 later became common in vernacular literature and Buddhist texts to describe a net spread both above and below, leaving no gap for escape.
example_zh: 警方布下了天罗地网，犯罪分子插翅难逃。
example_en: The police set up an inescapable dragnet; the criminals couldn't escape even if they had wings.

meaning: To look at flowers while riding a horse — meaning to give something a quick, superficial glance without taking in the details. It describes a hasty, cursory observation that misses the finer points.
origin: The idiom comes from a poem by the Tang dynasty poet Meng Jiao (孟郊) titled '登科后' (After Passing the Imperial Examination), written in 796 AD. Having finally passed the civil service exam at age forty-six, Meng Jiao rode his horse through the streets of Chang'an in high spirits, writing: '春风得意马蹄疾，一日看尽长安花' — 'Riding fast on spring breeze, I viewed all the flowers of Chang'an in a single day.' Later generations adapted this into the idiom '走马观花' to describe a rushed, superficial experience of things.
example_zh: 这次欧洲之行时间太短，不过是走马观花而已，很多景点都没来得及仔细游览。
example_en: The European trip was so short that it was just a quick glance — many attractions didn't get the thorough visit they deserved.

meaning: Refers to excessively flattering, coaxing, or honeyed words meant to deceive or please someone. It conveys that the speaker's kind-sounding words are insincere and often serve a manipulative purpose.
origin: The phrase appears in several classical Chinese works. One of the earliest recorded uses is found in the Yuan dynasty drama 《西厢记》 by Wang Shifu, where it describes characters using alluring speech to win favor. The concept of 'sweet words' as deceptive predates the idiom itself, appearing in texts such as the 《诗经》 (Book of Songs) and Han dynasty writings that warn against being swayed by pleasing rhetoric.
example_zh: 他总是用甜言蜜语骗取别人的信任，你可千万别上当。
example_en: He always uses sweet words to deceive people into trusting him—don't fall for it.

meaning: To willfully degrade oneself and give up all hope of self-improvement. It describes a person who, after setbacks or failures, loses confidence entirely and stops making any effort to better their situation.
origin: This idiom originates from the philosophical work 'Mengzi' (孟子), attributed to the Warring States period philosopher Mencius. Mencius wrote that a person who cannot be moved by words and who lacks the determination to cultivate goodness is '自暴者' (one who does violence to himself). He contrasted this with '自弃者' (one who abandons himself), stating that to forsake one's own moral nature is the greatest of self-destruction.
example_zh: 遇到一点挫折就自暴自弃，这样永远也无法成功。
example_en: Giving up on yourself at the first sign of setback means you will never succeed.

meaning: To stand together through hardship; sharing the same fate in times of adversity. It describes people who remain united and support one another despite facing severe difficulties or danger.
origin: This idiom originates from the ancient Chinese text "Sunzi's Art of War" (孙子兵法) by Sun Wu (孙武) of the Spring and Autumn period. In the chapter on military terrain, Sun Wu wrote that soldiers who share the same dangers — crossing wind and rain in the same boat — will unite as one. The passage reads: '夫吴人与越人相恶也，当其同舟而济，遇风，其相救也如左右手。' Later writers condensed this into the four-character idiom 风雨同舟.
example_zh: 在这次抗击疫情的斗争中，全国人民风雨同舟，共克时艰。
example_en: In the fight against the pandemic, people across the nation stood together through the storm and overcame the hardship as one.

meaning: To treat everyone with equal kindness and fairness, without discrimination or favoritism. It describes an attitude of impartial care toward all people, regardless of their status, background, or relationship to oneself.
origin: The idiom traces back to the thought of Mencius (孟子), the Warring States period philosopher. In the Mencian framework, a true ruler should extend benevolence (仁) equally to all subjects, just as a parent cares for all children alike. Later scholars and writers crystallized this ideal into the four-character expression 一视同仁, which became widely used in classical prose to praise impartial governance or universal compassion.
example_zh: 这位老师对每一个学生都一视同仁，从不偏袒任何人。
example_en: This teacher treats every student with equal fairness and never shows favoritism to anyone.

meaning: Describes something vast, boundless, and without limit — like the open sea and endless sky. It often conveys a sense of unrestrained freedom, whether in thought, conversation, or physical space. It can also describe someone who talks expansively about many topics without sticking to a point.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Tang dynasty poet Liu Zongyuan (柳宗元), who in his poem wrote of vast seas and skies to evoke a feeling of limitless openness. It was later popularized in Song dynasty literature to describe both expansive natural scenery and the unbounded nature of human thought. Over centuries it evolved into a common expression for unrestrained speech or imagination, used in both literary and everyday contexts.
example_zh: 两人在咖啡馆里聊得海阔天空，从天文地理一直谈到人生哲学。
example_en: The two chatted over coffee about everything under the sun, from astronomy and geography all the way to the philosophy of life.

literal: happy to hear, glad to see
meaning: This idiom describes something that people love to hear and see, referring to things that are widely popular and well-received by the masses. It is often used to describe cultural works, policies, or activities that resonate with and delight the general public.
origin: The phrase originates from the way classical Chinese thinkers discussed what kinds of things please common people. While it does not trace to a single specific historical anecdote, it gained widespread usage through Mao Zedong's 1942 Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art, where he emphasized that art and literature should be of the '喜闻乐见' variety — things the masses love to hear and gladly see — to truly serve the people. The idiom itself builds on classical Chinese patterns of parallel structure combining sensory verbs with emotion adjectives.
example_zh: 这部电影拍得通俗易懂，是老百姓喜闻乐见的好作品。
example_en: This film was made in an accessible style and is a great work that ordinary people love to watch.

meaning: Describes a place filled with an enormous, dense crowd of people. The sheer number of people makes the scene look like mountains of people and a sea of humanity stretching as far as the eye can see.
origin: This idiom appears in classical Chinese literature to vividly depict overwhelmingly large gatherings. The imagery of turning people into mountains and seas emphasizes both the height and breadth of a crowd. While no single definitive source text is universally cited, the expression grew from folk poetic conventions in the Ming and Qing dynasties and became standardized in modern Chinese idiom collections.
example_zh: 国庆节那天，天安门广场前人山人海，热闹非凡。
example_en: On National Day, the square in front of Tiananmen was absolutely packed with an enormous crowd, and the atmosphere was incredibly lively.

meaning: An extremely rare opportunity or event that might occur only once in a millennium. It emphasizes how precious and hard to come by a particular chance is, urging one to seize it.
origin: The phrase originates from classical Chinese literature and is commonly attributed to the Tang dynasty. It appears in works describing opportunities so rare they would not be encountered even over a span of a thousand years. The idiom crystallized through widespread literary usage across Tang and Song dynasty prose, where scholars and officials used it to describe extraordinary historical moments or once-in-a-lifetime encounters worth acting upon.
example_zh: 这次出国的机会千载难逢，你一定要好好把握。
example_en: This opportunity to go abroad is truly once in a lifetime — you must seize it.

meaning: To adopt measures suited to local conditions. It means that policies, methods, or strategies should be adapted to the specific circumstances and characteristics of each location rather than applied uniformly.
origin: The phrase appears in classical Chinese administrative and military writings. A closely related expression, 因地制宜宜, is attributed to discussions in the Han dynasty about governing diverse territories effectively. The core idea was championed by statesmen who argued that a one-size-fits-all approach to governance was bound to fail across China's vastly different regions.
example_zh: 各地气候和土壤条件差异很大，所以农业发展必须因地制宜，不能一刀切。
example_en: Climate and soil conditions vary greatly from place to place, so agricultural development must be adapted to local conditions rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

meaning: A chance meeting between strangers who happen to cross paths, much like duckweed drifting on water. It implies no prior connection and suggests the encounter is fleeting and may never be repeated. The idiom conveys a sense of transience and the randomness of human relationships.
origin: The phrase originates from a preface to a collection of poems by Wang Bo (王勃), a renowned poet of the early Tang dynasty. In his famous 'Preface to the Tengwang Pavilion' (滕王阁序, c. 675 AD), Wang Bo wrote '萍水相逢，尽是他乡之客' — 'Meeting like duckweed on water, all are guests from other lands.' Wang Bo composed this piece impromptu at a banquet held at Tengwang Pavilion in Jiangxi province, lamenting the impermanence of human encounters while traveling far from home.
example_zh: 我们在旅途中萍水相逢，却成了多年的好友。
example_en: We met by chance while traveling, yet became good friends for many years.

meaning: To live up to the expectations of the many; to not disappoint those who have placed their hopes in you. It conveys a sense of having fulfilled the trust or confidence that others have invested in a person or outcome.
origin: The phrase does not trace to a single classical text but crystallized from common literary usage combining 负 (to fail/betray) with 众望 (the people's expectations). Its conceptual roots appear in works like the Book of Later Han (后汉书), where officials were evaluated on whether they had 让众人失望 or not. Over centuries the concise four-character form 不负众望 became standard in late imperial and modern written Chinese.
example_zh: 他不负众望，在全国比赛中获得了金牌。
example_en: He lived up to everyone's expectations and won the gold medal in the national competition.

meaning: An idiom describing a woman of such extraordinary beauty that she could cause the downfall of an entire state or city. It is used to praise a woman's unparalleled, world-class beauty in a poetic and dramatic way.
origin: The phrase originates from a poem by the Han dynasty scholar Li Yannian (李延年) presented to Emperor Wu of Han (汉武帝). The poem reads: "北方有佳人，绝世而独立。一顾倾人城，再顾倾人国。" (In the north there is a lovely one, unique in the world. One glance overthrows a city, a second glance overthrows a state.) The emperor was so moved that he asked to meet this beauty, and Li Yannian introduced his sister, Lady Li (李夫人), who became one of the emperor's favorite consorts.
example_zh: 她倾国倾城的容貌让在场的所有人都为之倾倒。
example_en: Her devastatingly beautiful appearance left everyone present completely captivated.

meaning: Describes a person who is dressed immaculately and elegantly, with every garment in perfect order. It conveys a well-groomed, polished appearance that draws attention. The idiom is generally neutral in tone, though it can sometimes carry a slight ironic undertone when applied to someone whose inner character does not match their outward elegance.
origin: The phrase traces back to the Shi Jing (Classic of Poetry, c. 11th–7th century BCE), specifically the poem "Qi Feng - Zi Yi" in the "Zheng Feng" section. The original lines read "蜉蝣之羽，衣裳楚楚" (The mayfly's wings, its garments are fine and neat), using the ephemeral mayfly as a metaphor for the fragile splendor of noble attire. Later literary tradition expanded the usage from describing garments alone to characterizing the overall appearance of a well-dressed person, as seen in works from the Ming and Qing dynasties.
example_zh: 他今天衣冠楚楚地出席了晚宴，整个人显得格外精神。
example_en: He attended the banquet immaculately dressed today, looking exceptionally sharp and polished.

meaning: To be wholeheartedly devoted to something with undivided attention and complete sincerity. It describes someone who focuses entirely on a single task, goal, or person without any distraction or second thought.
origin: The idiom appears in multiple classical texts. A notable early usage is found in the Guanzi (管子), a text attributed to Guan Zhong (管仲) of the Spring and Autumn period, which states that a ruler must concentrate his will without wavering. The phrase also appears in Zhuangzi (庄子) and later works, consistently conveying the idea that unity of heart and mind leads to success and moral clarity.
example_zh: 他一心一意地投入到科研工作中，几年如一日。
example_en: He devoted himself wholeheartedly to his research work, day in and day out for years.

meaning: To be solved with ease, as if a bamboo stalk naturally splits apart when the blade finds its edge. It describes a situation where, once the key point or main obstacle is addressed, everything else falls into place effortlessly.
origin: This idiom comes from the Jin Shu (Book of Jin), in the biography of Du Yu (杜预), a prominent general and scholar of the Western Jin dynasty. When Emperor Wu of Jin planned to conquer the state of Eastern Wu, many officials opposed the campaign. Du Yu persistently advocated for it, arguing that once the main forces struck, the enemy's resistance would collapse like bamboo splitting along its natural seams. The campaign succeeded in 280 AD, unifying China, and Du Yu's metaphor of splitting bamboo gave rise to the idiom.
example_zh: 只要找到问题的关键所在，其他难题就会迎刃而解。
example_en: As long as we find the crux of the problem, all the other difficulties will be easily solved.

meaning: Describes something so extraordinary, mysterious, or profound that it defies ordinary understanding or imagination. It conveys a sense of awe at something beyond the reach of human reasoning, whether wondrous or dreadful.
origin: This idiom traces back to the Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra (《维摩诘所说经》), a Mahāyāna Buddhist text translated into Chinese during the Eastern Jin dynasty by Kumārajīva. In Buddhist philosophy, '不可思议' refers to the ineffable nature of ultimate truth (dharma) that cannot be grasped through ordinary conceptual thought. Over centuries the phrase entered secular Chinese, shedding its strictly religious connotation and becoming a common expression for anything that strains belief.
example_zh: 这座古城在地下沉睡了上千年，保存之完好简直不可思议。
example_en: This ancient city lay dormant underground for over a thousand years; its remarkable state of preservation is truly inconceivable.

meaning: To add trouble to someone who is already in difficulty, or to kick someone when they are down. It describes the despicable act of making matters worse for a person who is already in a desperate or vulnerable situation.
origin: The idiom derives from a passage in the Tang dynasty essay 'To Wang Feng' (《答王凤书》) by the renowned poet and official Han Yu (韩愈). Han Yu wrote that when someone falls into a well, some people not only fail to help but even throw stones down after them. This metaphor powerfully condemned those who exploit others' misfortune.
example_zh: 他都已经失业了，你还在背后说他的坏话，这不是落井下石吗？
example_en: He's already lost his job, and you're still badmouthing him behind his back — isn't that kicking him while he's down?

meaning: To forge ahead despite knowing the difficulties ahead. It describes a courageous and resolute attitude of facing challenges head-on rather than retreating when the path is hard.
origin: The phrase derives from classical Chinese philosophical thought, particularly associated with the Confucian tradition. The idea of advancing in the face of difficulty is echoed in the Analects (论语), where Confucius taught that a noble person presses forward despite knowing the enormity of the task. The four-character formulation became a standard idiom used in later dynasties to praise determination and moral courage.
example_zh: 面对技术瓶颈，团队选择知难而进，最终成功突破了难关。
example_en: Faced with a technical bottleneck, the team chose to forge ahead despite the difficulties and ultimately succeeded in breaking through the barrier.

meaning: A single promise is as valuable as a thousand pieces of gold. It describes a person who keeps their word faithfully and whose promises can be completely trusted.
origin: This idiom originates from the Western Han dynasty and is associated with Ji Bu (季布), a general famous for his loyalty and trustworthiness. A popular saying of the time stated, 'Getting a hundred catties of gold is not as good as getting one promise from Ji Bu.' The phrase was later recorded in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史记) in the biography of Ji Bu, cementing it as a classical expression of integrity.
example_zh: 他是个一诺千金的人，答应过的事情一定会做到。
example_en: He is a man whose word is as good as gold — whatever he promises, he will definitely deliver.

meaning: Describes music or singing so beautiful that its sound seems to linger in the air long after it has stopped. It is used metaphorically to praise performances or speeches that leave a deep, lasting impression on the audience.
origin: This idiom comes from the ancient text "Liezi" (《列子·汤问》), attributed to the Warring States period. It tells of Han E (韩娥), a brilliant singer from the state of Han, who passed through the state of Qi. After she left a tavern where she had sung, people felt her voice still echoing around the rafters for days, unable to forget the beauty of her song. Later, when she sang a mournful tune in a village, the entire community wept for three days straight.
example_zh: 她那首咏叹调唱得真是余音绕梁，三日不绝，让在场所有人都沉醉其中。
example_en: Her aria lingered in the air for what felt like days, leaving everyone in the audience completely entranced.

meaning: This idiom describes the belief that beautiful women often suffer unfortunate or tragic destinies. It reflects the classical Chinese notion that extraordinary beauty invites misfortune rather than happiness. The phrase is used to express sympathy or lamentation when a beautiful woman encounters hardship or an early death.
origin: The sentiment appears in classical literature from the Tang dynasty onward, notably in Bai Juyi's poem 'Song of Everlasting Sorrow' (《长恨歌》) about the tragic fate of Imperial Consort Yang Guifei, whose beauty led to her downfall. The phrase itself crystallized from earlier folk wisdom and poetic tradition that linked feminine beauty with vulnerability to misfortune. It became a recurring motif in Chinese drama, poetry, and fiction as a shorthand for the tragic arc of beautiful female characters.
example_zh: 自古红颜薄命，她年纪轻轻就身患重病，实在令人惋惜。
example_en: As the saying goes, beautiful women suffer tragic fates; it is truly heartbreaking that she fell gravely ill at such a young age.

meaning: Describes someone who is supremely arrogant and considers no one else as important as themselves. It conveys an attitude of absolute self-importance, where the person believes they are above everyone else and refuses to acknowledge the worth or authority of others.
origin: This idiom traces back to Buddhist scriptures recounting the birth of Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha). According to legend, upon being born, the infant Buddha took seven steps, pointed one hand toward the sky and one toward the earth, and declared, '天上天下，唯我独尊' — 'In heaven and on earth, I alone am the honored one.' Originally this expressed the Buddha's unique and supreme spiritual status. Over time, the phrase shed its religious context and became a general term for extreme arrogance and self-centeredness.
example_zh: 他总是一副唯我独尊的样子，从不把别人的意见放在眼里。
example_en: He always acts as though he alone matters, never giving anyone else's opinion a second thought.

meaning: Describes a state of being completely relaxed and joyful, with a broad and open mind. It conveys the feeling of contentment that comes from being in a beautiful natural setting or free from worldly worries.
origin: This idiom comes from the Song Dynasty essay 'Yueyang Tower' (《岳阳楼记》) by the renowned statesman and writer Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹). In the essay, Fan describes how gazing out over the vast expanse of Lake Dongting on a clear spring day, with gentle breezes and bright sunshine, makes one feel '心旷神怡, 宠辱偕忘' — broad of heart and delighted in spirit, forgetting both favor and disgrace. The essay, written in 1046, is one of the most celebrated works of classical Chinese prose.
example_zh: 登上山顶，俯瞰云海翻涌，不禁令人心旷神怡。
example_en: Reaching the mountaintop and gazing down at the rolling sea of clouds, one cannot help but feel completely relaxed and joyful.

meaning: Describes something so solid and strong that it absolutely cannot be broken, crushed, or destroyed. It is used both literally for physical fortifications and metaphorically for an unshakable will, belief, or alliance.
origin: The idiom appears in early historical and military texts describing impenetrable defenses. A notable classical usage is found in accounts of the Six Dynasties period, where historians described the formidable defenses of key cities and fortresses that withstood prolonged sieges. The phrase crystallized from common military language of the time into a fixed four-character idiom used to convey absolute invincibility, whether of walls, armies, or resolve.
example_zh: 这支军队纪律严明、团结一致，形成了一道坚不可摧的钢铁防线。
example_en: This army, with its strict discipline and unity, formed an indestructible line of steel.

meaning: An idiom describing a scene full of the songs of birds and the scent of flowers. It is used to paint a vivid picture of a beautiful, lively spring landscape. By extension, it conveys a pleasant, harmonious, and idyllic atmosphere.
origin: The phrase traces its roots to classical Chinese literary descriptions of spring scenery rather than a single historical anecdote. It appears in various forms in Tang and Song dynasty poetry and prose celebrating the beauty of nature. The pairing of birdsong and floral fragrance became a stock literary image for an ideal spring day. Over centuries of literary use, the four-character collocation solidified into a fixed idiom.
example_zh: 春天的公园里鸟语花香，吸引了许多市民前来散步赏景。
example_en: The spring park was filled with birdsong and the fragrance of flowers, attracting many citizens who came to stroll and enjoy the scenery.

meaning: To endure all kinds of hardships and suffering. It describes someone who bears great difficulties patiently, often for the sake of others or a higher purpose, without complaint.
origin: The idiom traces its roots to Song dynasty literature, where both 含辛 and 茹苦 appeared independently in earlier classical texts such as the Book of Songs (诗经) and Songs of Chu (楚辞). The combined form 含辛茹苦 became widely used in Song-era writings to describe the suffering of parents raising children or the hardships of devoted service. It has since become a standard idiom for patient endurance of adversity.
example_zh: 母亲含辛茹苦地把我们兄妹三人拉扯大，从没抱怨过一句。
example_en: My mother endured untold hardships to raise the three of us, yet never uttered a single complaint.

meaning: Describes something, usually gratitude, love, or a painful experience, that is so deeply felt it seems carved into one's very bones and engraved upon one's heart. It conveys an impression or memory that can never be forgotten.
origin: The idiom has roots in classical literature. The component 铭心 appears in Tang dynasty poetry, such as in Li Bai's work, meaning words engraved on the heart. The fuller pairing 刻骨 with 铭心 developed over centuries of literary usage, appearing in various Song and Ming dynasty texts to describe unforgettable feelings, especially deep gratitude or sorrow.
example_zh: 那份恩情让我刻骨铭心，一辈子都不会忘记。
example_en: That kindness left an indelible mark on me—I will never forget it as long as I live.

meaning: To satisfy both sides of a situation, achieving the best outcome for everyone involved. It describes a solution or arrangement where two parties both get what they want, leaving neither side shortchanged. The phrase emphasizes harmony and mutual benefit in a dilemma that otherwise forces a trade-off.
origin: The idiom traces back to the Ming dynasty novel 'Xingshi Hengyan' (醒世恒言) by Feng Menglong. In one story, a clever intermediary arranges a marriage that resolves a family conflict, pleasing both the groom's family and the bride's family simultaneously. The phrase became shorthand for any win-win resolution where no compromise diminishes either party.
example_zh: 这个方案既降低了成本，又提高了效率，真是两全其美的好办法。
example_en: This plan both cuts costs and boosts efficiency — truly a solution that achieves the best of both worlds.

meaning: Describes a situation that keeps getting progressively worse over time. It conveys a steady and seemingly relentless decline from an already poor state.
origin: This idiom evolved from a passage in the Daoist text Zhuangzi (庄子·知北游), in which Zhuangzi's disciple Dao Jian asks about the Dao and is told to observe it in increasingly lowly places — from ants and weeds to excrement and urine — meaning the Dao is present even in the most degraded states. The original phrase was "每下愈况" (měi xià yù kuàng), literally 'the further down you go, the more evident it becomes.' Over time, later generations misread and reordered it as "每况愈下," and the meaning shifted from a philosophical point about finding truth everywhere to simply describing a downward spiral.
example_zh: 这家公司的经营状况每况愈下，连续三个季度亏损，裁员也在持续扩大。
example_en: This company's business conditions have gone from bad to worse, posting losses for three consecutive quarters while layoffs continue to expand.

meaning: To break through thorny undergrowth on a difficult path, metaphorically meaning to overcome great obstacles and hardships to forge ahead. It describes clearing away all barriers in pursuit of a goal with courage and determination.
origin: This idiom traces back to the Eastern Han dynasty. The founder of Eastern Han, Emperor Guangwu (Liu Xiu), sent his general Feng Yi on a military campaign. Feng Yi described the hardships of his march, saying he had to cut through thorns and brambles to open the way. The phrase was later recorded in the Book of Later Han (《后汉书·冯异传》), where it became a literary expression for forging a path through extreme difficulty.
example_zh: 创业初期，他们披荆斩棘，终于把公司做大做强了。
example_en: In the early days of starting the business, they overcame countless obstacles and finally built the company into a major success.

meaning: Describes an enormous, formidable military force or a vast crowd of people and things. It conveys a sense of overwhelming scale and power, often used metaphorically for any massive movement or grand spectacle.
origin: The phrase appears in Tang dynasty literature, notably in Han Yu's (韩愈) essay 'Lun Tianxia Shi Ren' (论天下史人), where he wrote of vast armies on campaign. The idiom crystallized through classical military writings and historical records that routinely described imperial campaigns in terms of 'thousands of troops and tens of thousands of horses,' reflecting the immense scale of warfare in ancient China.
example_zh: 面对千军万马的敌军，他毫无惧色，镇定自若地指挥着部队。
example_en: Facing the enemy's mighty force of thousands of troops and horses, he showed no fear and calmly directed his troops.

meaning: To have a well-thought-out plan or a clear picture in mind before taking action. It describes someone who is fully prepared and confident because they have already envisioned the desired outcome.
origin: This idiom comes from the Song Dynasty painter Wen Tong (文同), who was renowned for his bamboo ink paintings. According to Su Shi's writings, Wen Tong would observe bamboo carefully in all seasons and conditions until he could picture the entire bamboo in his mind before ever lifting his brush. Su Shi praised him by saying that when Wen Tong painted bamboo, he already had the complete image of bamboo in his chest.
example_zh: 面对这场复杂的谈判，他早已胸有成竹，提出的方案让所有人都信服。
example_en: Facing this complex negotiation, he already had a well-thought-out plan, and the proposal he put forward convinced everyone.

meaning: Being well-prepared in advance prevents danger or trouble. It emphasizes that taking precautions before problems arise is the best way to avoid harm. The idiom advocates proactive planning rather than reactive problem-solving.
origin: This idiom originates from the Zuo Zhuan (左传), a foundational historical text covering the Spring and Autumn period (722–468 BC). In the passage, the statesman Shi Kuang (师旷) advises that one should prepare for adversity before it arrives, drawing a parallel to storing grain before famine. The full classical phrase reads '有备无患' directly. The text is attributed to Zuo Qiuming and records the history of the state of Lu.
example_zh: 出门前检查一下天气预报，有备无患嘛。
example_en: Check the weather forecast before heading out — better safe than sorry.

meaning: An idiom referring to the facts or the rights and wrongs of a situation. When used in the negative (e.g., 不分青红皂白, 'without distinguishing blue from red, black from white'), it means acting recklessly or making judgments without first understanding the truth of the matter.
origin: The phrase appears in various forms in vernacular literature of the Ming and Qing dynasties. It draws on the ancient Chinese color system, where 青 (blue/green), 红 (red), 皂 (black), and 白 (white) represented the most fundamental color distinctions. The idiom uses these basic color categories as a metaphor for the fundamental facts or truth of a situation — just as one would distinguish one color from another, one should distinguish right from wrong before acting. A notable early usage appears in the Ming dynasty novel 'Water Margin' (水浒传), where characters are described as acting without distinguishing 青红皂白.
example_zh: 他连事情的原委都没搞清楚，就不分青红皂白地把人训斥了一顿。
example_en: He hadn't even figured out what happened before he started chewing people out, making no distinction between right and wrong.

meaning: Describes someone who is extremely meticulous and thorough in everything they do, not neglecting even the smallest detail. It conveys a strict, earnest attitude toward work or tasks, where nothing is overlooked or done sloppily.
origin: This idiom comes from the Qing dynasty scholar Wu Jingzi's satirical novel "Rulin Waishi" (The Scholars), also known as "儒林外史". In Chapter 42, the text describes a character's calligraphy as so precise and careful that not a single stroke was careless, using the phrase to praise the highest level of diligence in craft and scholarship. Wu Jingzi used it to illustrate the ideal attitude of a dedicated scholar who attends to every minute detail.
example_zh: 王老师批改作业一丝不苟，连一个标点符号的错误都不会放过。
example_en: Teacher Wang grades homework with meticulous care — he won't let even a single punctuation mistake slip by.

meaning: Describes a state of great anxiety, nervousness, or inner turmoil where one's emotions fluctuate unpredictably. It conveys the feeling of being unsettled, unable to find peace of mind.
origin: This idiom has roots in classical Chinese numerological and folk traditions. The phrase appears in early vernacular literature, including works from the Ming dynasty such as Journey to the West (西游记), where it is used to depict characters' restless, wavering states of mind. The numbers seven and eight were often used colloquially to suggest disorder or instability, and the contrasting directions 'up' and 'down' vividly capture the image of a heart bouncing erratically. Over time it became a standard expression for anxiety and emotional unease in spoken and written Chinese.
example_zh: 得知考试结果还没公布，她心里七上八下的，坐立不安。
example_en: With the exam results not yet announced, she was on edge and couldn't sit still.

meaning: Something happens suddenly and unexpectedly, without any warning or preparation. It describes an event or situation that catches people completely off guard, like a bolt from the blue.
origin: This idiom traces back to the ancient Chinese philosophical text "Liji" (Book of Rites, 礼记), compiled during the Western Han dynasty (206 BC–9 AD), specifically in the chapter "Tan Gong" (檀弓). It originally described death arriving without forewarning, emphasizing that life's most momentous events can strike at any time. The passage reads: "出乎尔者，反乎尔者也; 如此者，突如其来如，焚如，死如，弃如."
example_zh: 这场暴雨突如其来，让街上的人纷纷四处躲避。
example_en: The rainstorm came out of nowhere, sending people on the street scurrying for cover.

meaning: Describes things that change and improve rapidly and constantly. It conveys the idea of continuous, rapid progress or transformation in a very positive sense.
origin: This idiom comes from the 'Book of Rites' (《礼记·大学》), one of the Five Classics of Confucianism. The original text states: '苟日新，日日新，又日新' (If you can improve yourself in a day, do so each day, building always upon the previous day's improvement). Later scholars elaborated this idea into '日新月异', expanding the notion of daily renewal to monthly transformation. The phrase has been used since ancient times to describe both moral self-improvement and the rapid advancement of civilization, technology, or society.
example_zh: 随着科技的发展，人们的生活方式日新月异。
example_en: With the development of technology, people's lifestyles change rapidly and constantly.

literal: drive light carriage, follow familiar road
meaning: To do something with ease because one is experienced and familiar with it. It describes the confidence and fluency that come from long practice or deep familiarity with a task.
origin: This idiom comes from a letter by the Tang dynasty official Han Yu (韩愈) titled '送石处士序' (Preface on Bidding Farewell to Scholar Shi). Han Yu wrote that a skilled horseman driving a light carriage on a familiar road feels no strain, using this metaphor to describe someone who applies their expertise effortlessly. The phrase has been used ever since to praise seasoned competence.
example_zh: 他在这行干了二十年，处理这类问题自然是驾轻就熟。
example_en: He's been in this industry for twenty years, so handling these kinds of problems is naturally a breeze for him.

meaning: To make a fool of oneself before an expert or a knowledgeable audience. It conveys humility or self-deprecation, acknowledging that one's limited skill or knowledge may seem laughable to those who truly understand the subject.
origin: The phrase comes from Zhuangzi (《庄子·秋水》), where the River God, having swelled with pride after the autumn flood, ventures to the North Sea for the first time. There he meets Ruo (若), the spirit of the sea, whose vastness makes the river feel utterly insignificant. Ruo remarks that one cannot discuss the ocean with a well frog, and the idiom emerged from this theme of the ignorant presuming to instruct the knowledgeable.
example_zh: 在各位专家面前班门弄斧，实在是贻笑大方。
example_en: Showing off my meager skills in front of all these experts is truly making a fool of myself.

meaning: Describes someone who speaks with great eloquence and fluency, as if water were pouring endlessly from their mouth. It typically conveys admiration for a person's oratorical skill and ability to talk at length on a subject without hesitation.
origin: The idiom comes from the Jin Dynasty scholar Guo Xiang (郭象), as recorded in the Shishuo Xinyu (世说新语) by Liu Yiqing. Guo Xiang was renowned for his brilliant philosophical discourses, and his contemporary Wang Yan (王衍) praised him by saying his speech flowed like a torrential river pouring down from a cliff — never stopping, never faltering. The phrase was later crystallized into the four-character idiom 口若悬河.
example_zh: 他在辩论赛上口若悬河，把对手驳得哑口无言。
example_en: He spoke with the eloquence of a raging river at the debate, leaving his opponent completely speechless.

meaning: An enormous, awe-inspiring object or creature. It describes something of massive size that can appear imposing or intimidating, sometimes with the implication that its great size may belie actual strength or capability.
origin: This idiom comes from Tang dynasty writer Liu Zongyuan's fable '三戒' (Three Admonitions), specifically the story '黔之驴' (The Donkey of Guizhou). A donkey from elsewhere is brought to Guizhou province, where a tiger has never seen one before. The tiger observes this 庞然大物 from a distance, initially terrified by its enormous size and loud braying, but eventually discovers the donkey has no real fighting skills and devours it. The phrase has since been used to describe anything of great size.
example_zh: 那头大象站在草原上，真是一个庞然大物，让人望而生畏。
example_en: The elephant standing on the grassland was a truly massive creature, inspiring awe and fear at the sight of it.

meaning: To not hesitate at all; to be willing to do something regardless of the cost or sacrifice. It conveys a resolute attitude of not grudging any effort, money, or even one's life to achieve a goal.
origin: The phrase has deep classical Chinese roots, combining the grammatical structure found in earlier texts. The components appear in contexts where scholars and officials declared their willingness to sacrifice everything for loyalty or a righteous cause. It crystallized as a fixed expression in Ming and Qing dynasty literature, frequently used in historical novels and essays to describe figures who accepted any cost for duty or principle.
example_zh: 为了国家的安全，即使牺牲个人生命，也在所不惜。
example_en: For the sake of national security, they would not hesitate even if it meant sacrificing their own lives.

meaning: Describes a state of restlessness and anxiety, where one's heart pounds nervously and one cannot feel calm. It conveys both physical unease and mental worry, often in anticipation of uncertain news or outcomes.
